A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FocalCodec study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original resynthesis, voice-conversion, downstream-task, ablation, streaming, and listening-test results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional causal-streaming and FSQ-ablation results, alongside revised TTS and listening-test outcomes.

M1.justification: The original offline architecture is retained, but v2 Appendix G.3 introduces a causal variant, replacing non-causal components, distilling non-causal WavLM features through a feature-matching loss, and training a 24 kHz decoder. v1 evaluated only non-causal chunked streaming and identified a fully causal architecture as future work.

E1.justification: The named datasets, languages, and downstream tasks are retained, and streaming was already evaluated in v1. However, v2 Appendix G.3 mentions additional training data for the causal variant without identifying their source or domain. It is unclear whether this expands coverage or merely increases data quantity within existing coverage.

E2.justification: The main codec roster and TS3-Codec comparison remain unchanged. v2 adds FSQ to the quantizer ablation and EnCodec and Mimi to the streaming comparison. The WavLM6-KM continuous-input comparison disappears with the removed speech-separation analysis.

E3.justification: v2 excludes TTS test utterances longer than 20 seconds, approximately 4% of test-clean. The listening study changes from 21 participants to 40 submissions, retaining 33 after a minimum-listening-time filter. The new causal experiment uses 24 kHz output, 4096 codes, and 80 ms latency. Table 1 also revises Stable Codec's reported size from 95M to 950M parameters while retaining the identified checkpoint; this does not establish a replacement or rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a BSQ-versus-FSQ quality and code-entropy ablation but removes the Vocos-versus-HiFi-GAN comparison. It deletes v1 Appendix F.4 and Table 10, which tested whether continuous input alleviates speech-separation failures. The streaming analysis drops the shorter-chunk and lower-token-rate sensitivity results and adds a causal-model comparison.

E5.justification: Figure 2 changes its stated distribution summary from red median markers in v1 to red mean markers in v2. Both versions show listener-score distributions; neither introduces training-seed repetitions, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The participant-count and screening changes concern evaluation design.

E6.justification: Resynthesis, voice-conversion, and non-TTS downstream scores remain unchanged. TTS results are replaced under revised evaluation conditions: FocalCodec@25 dWER changes from 30.28 to 16.75, and the preferred TTS variant changes from @12.5 to @25; these are not same-setting gains. v2 adds causal-streaming results of 3.87 UTMOS, 4.38 dWER, and 96.3 Sim at 80 ms, adds FSQ results, updates listening-score distributions, and removes several diagnostic result entries.

T1.justification: The focal-modulation equation and binary spherical quantization definitions in Equations 1–4 are unchanged. v2 adds explanatory prose but no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: focal modulation, a single binary codebook operating at 0.16–0.65 kbps, competitive reconstruction and voice conversion, and preservation of semantic and acoustic information for downstream tasks.

C2.justification: v2 explains rising UTMOS at lower bitrates through smoothing and cautions about metric saturation. It substantially revises real-time applicability through the causal variant, removes the detailed speech-separation bottleneck interpretation, and drops the explicit music/environmental-audio limitation. Appendix A emphasizes undertraining, while the new societal-impact section discusses communication benefits and voice-conversion misuse.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset and baseline licenses, a link to the selected multilingual evaluation data, and clarifications about DAC's checkpoint and the ablation decoder. Appendix E.2 first documents generating five TTS candidates and selecting the lowest-Whisper-WER candidate; v1 does not establish whether this procedure was already used. The new causal variant's exact capacity and training data remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds BASE TTS, FireRedTTS, and MaskGCT when contrasting continuous speaker/prosody embeddings with unified discrete representations. It also cites ESPnet-SpeechLM for TTS candidate selection and distinguishes contrastive from predictive pretraining. The broader acoustic/semantic/hybrid positioning remains intact; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include expanded focal-modulation and training/inference explanations, rewritten limitations, new societal-impact and acknowledgments sections, reordered appendix analyses, and affiliation and citation-style edits.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, substantially reflowing and resizing displays. Clean and noisy resynthesis tables are merged; bitrate columns are added; ablation and streaming tables are redesigned; and the baseline table gains licenses. Figure 2 is updated and v1 Table 10 is removed. Figures 1 and 3 retain their content with changed sizing.

improvement.justification: The larger screened listening study, direct FSQ comparison, and reported causal-streaming experiment strengthen empirical support, while the UTMOS caveat improves interpretation. The gains are limited by unspecified causal-model capacity and training data, narrower TTS testing with newly documented candidate selection, and removal of useful decoder, streaming-sensitivity, and speech-separation diagnostics. Overall, v2 offers a supported but limited quality improvement.
